title: Turbulent Flow in Fluids
short_intro: Turbulent flow is a fluid motion regime characterized by chaotic changes in pressure and flow velocity, unlike laminar flow where fluids flow in parallel layers. It occurs at high Reynolds numbers where inertial forces dominate over viscous forces.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of turbulent flow, distinction from streamline and laminar flow, critical velocity, and Reynolds number formula with its dimensionless nature.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Navier-Stokes equation applications in high Reynolds number limits, eddy viscosity, Prandtl mixing length theory, and Kolmogorov's theory of turbulence.

prerequisites: Equation of continuity and Bernoulli's theorem

concept_notes.heading: Characteristics of Turbulent Flow
bullets: Fluid particles move in a zig-zag, irregular, and haphazard path leading to rapid mixing.
Velocity at any point in the fluid fluctuates randomly in both magnitude and direction with time.
Energy dissipation is significantly higher than in laminar flow due to internal fluid friction caused by eddies.

concept_notes.heading: Reynolds Number (Re)
bullets: A dimensionless quantity used to predict flow transition in different fluid flow situations.
Defined mathematically as Re = (ρvd)/(η) or Re = (vd)/(ν), where ρ is density, v is velocity, d is characteristic length, η is dynamic viscosity, and ν is kinematic viscosity.
For flow through a cylindrical pipe, Re < 2000 indicates laminar flow, 2000 < Re < 3000 represents an unstable transition state, and Re > 3000 ensures fully developed turbulent flow.

concept_notes.heading: Critical Velocity
bullets: Defined as the maximum velocity of fluid flow up to which the flow remains streamline or laminar.
If the velocity exceeds this critical value, the smooth flow breaks down and becomes turbulent.
Depends directly on the viscosity and inversely on the density and radius of the pipe.

concept_notes.heading: Role of Inertial and Viscous Forces
bullets: Inertial forces tend to perpetuate the velocity fluctuations and spatial disorder of fluid elements.
Viscous forces act to damp out velocity gradients and suppress small-scale fluctuations, maintaining order.
Turbulence dominates when inertial forces vastly overwhelm the stabilizing viscous forces.

derivations.title: Dimensional Analysis of Reynolds Number
derivations.conditions: Incompressible fluid flow in a straight cylindrical pipe
steps: Assume critical velocity (v) depends on fluid density (ρ), dynamic viscosity (η), and pipe diameter (d).
Equate powers of M, L, and T: For M: a + b = 0; For L: -3a - b + c = 1; For T: -b = -1.
Solve for constants: b = 1, a = -1, c = -1.
Substitute back to get the proportionality: v ∝ η / (ρd), which rearranges to (ρvd)/(η) = constant.

derivations.title: Head Loss in Turbulent Pipe Flow (Darcy-Weisbach Relation)
derivations.conditions: Fully developed turbulent flow in a constant diameter horizontal pipe
steps: Consider shear stress at the pipe wall (τ<sub>w</sub>) balancing the pressure drop (ΔP).
Express pressure force as (ΔP)(πd<sup>2</sup>)/4 and frictional force as τ<sub>w</sub>(πd)L.
Introduce the Darcy friction factor f where τ<sub>w</sub> = (f/8)ρv<sup>2</sup>.
Substitute τ<sub>w</sub> into the pressure drop equation to obtain head loss h<sub>f</sub>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reynolds' Dye Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic showing a glass pipe with water flow from a reservoir, injecting a fine filament of colored dye at the entrance. At low flow, the dye forms a straight line; at high flow, it diffuses completely.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the transition from laminar flow (straight dye streak) to turbulent flow (dispersed, mixing dye streak) as velocity increases.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual questions regarding the critical velocity and visual confirmation of turbulence.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Friction Factor vs Reynolds Number (Moody Diagram Sketch)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Log-log plot of friction factor f against Reynolds number Re. Shows a downward sloping curve for laminar region (f = 64/Re) and distinct curves for varying relative roughness in the turbulent zone.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that in turbulent flow, friction factor depends on both Reynolds number and pipe wall roughness, unlike laminar flow.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting parameter dependencies in fluid friction problems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Distribution Profile
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Comparison of parabolic velocity profile (laminar) versus a flattened, blunt velocity profile across a pipe diameter for turbulent flow.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Turbulent flow exhibits a much more uniform velocity distribution across the central core of the pipe due to rapid momentum mixing by eddies.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: MCQs contrasting laminar and turbulent velocity profiles.

solved_numericals.question: Water at 20°C flows through a pipe of diameter 0.05 m. If the density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and dynamic viscosity is 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, what is the maximum velocity for laminar flow? (Assume critical Reynolds number is 2000)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: d = 0.05 m, ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, η = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, Re = 2000.
Use the critical velocity formula: v_c = (Re * η) / (ρ * d).
Calculate the result: v_c = 2 / 50 = 0.04 m s⁻¹.

solved_numericals.question: Air with density 1.2 kg m⁻³ and kinematic viscosity 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹ flows through a large ventilation duct of diameter 2.0 m. Calculate the Reynolds number when the average flow velocity is 5 m s⁻¹ and determine the flow regime.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: v = 5 m s⁻¹, d = 2.0 m, ν = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹.
Use the Reynolds number formula involving kinematic viscosity: Re = (v * d) / ν.
Compare with threshold: Since Re >> 3000, the flow is highly turbulent.

solved_numericals.question: Oil of density 900 kg m⁻³ and dynamic viscosity 0.1 Pa s flows through a pipe of diameter 0.1 m at a velocity of 2 m s⁻¹. Find the head loss due to friction over a length of 50 m using the friction factor relationship f = 64/Re for laminar, or appropriate turbulent correlation if applicable.
solution_steps: Calculate Reynolds number: Re = (ρ * v * d) / η = (900 * 2 * 0.1) / 0.1 = 1800.
Since Re = 1800 (< 2000), the flow is actually laminar. Use laminar friction factor f = 64 / Re.
Apply Darcy-Weisbach equation for head loss: h_f = (f * L * v²) / (2 * g * d).
solved_numericals.answer: 3.63 m (Note: Flow verified as laminar despite turbulent context)

assumptions_and_limitations: Navier-Stokes equations apply universally, but exact analytical solutions for turbulent flow are intractable due to non-linearity and three-dimensional vorticity fluctuations, necessitating statistical or empirical models.
The Reynolds number threshold (Re = 2000 to 3000) is empirical and depends heavily on pipe entrance conditions, wall roughness, and external vibrations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Turbulent flow has a constant velocity at any given point if averaged over time.
common_misconceptions.correct: Velocity fluctuates randomly and persistently around a mean value in turbulent flow.
common_misconceptions.why: Turbulence is inherently unsteady at small time scales, even if macroscopic boundary conditions are steady.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Viscosity plays no role in turbulent flow since inertial forces dominate.
common_misconceptions.correct: Viscosity remains crucial in the microscopic boundary layer (viscous sublayer) and dictates energy dissipation at the Kolmogorov microscale.
common_misconceptions.why: Viscous dissipation is the ultimate mechanism converting kinetic energy of turbulence into internal thermal energy.

quick_revision: Turbulent flow occurs when the Reynolds number exceeds approximately 3000 in pipe flow.
Critical velocity is inversely proportional to fluid density and pipe radius, and directly proportional to viscosity.
Darcy-Weisbach equation relates head loss directly to pipe length and square of velocity, and inversely to pipe diameter.
